stem:
Which part of the sentence has an error? If the sentence is correct, choose "No error".

Every Monday, the seminar for new employees starts on 9:00 a.m.
hints: Look at the small words that come before a time: at, on, in. Each one goes with a different kind of time.
"9:00 a.m." is a clock time. Which small word goes with a clock time?
Rule: AT a clock time (at 3:30), ON a day or date (on Monday, on May 5), IN a month, a year or a part of the day (in June, in 2026, in the morning). Check each part.

solution.methodName: Match at, on or in to the kind of time

steps.action: Find the time words: "Every Monday" and "9:00 a.m.".
"9:00 a.m." is a clock time, and clock times take "at".
steps.why: Use "at" for clock times, "on" for days and dates, and "in" for months and years.

steps.action: Check "Every Monday". It is correct with no "on".
steps.why: With every, next or last, you drop the preposition: every Monday, next week, last year.

steps.action: Check "for new employees". It tells who the seminar is for, and it is correct.
The error is "starts on 9:00 a.m.". It should be "starts at 9:00 a.m.".

trapNotes.Every Monday: Some think it needs "On" in front. But with every, next and last, no preposition is needed: every Monday, next week.
trapNotes.for new employees: This part is correct. "A seminar for new employees" uses "for" to show who it is meant for.
trapNotes.No error: "On" is right for days, so "on 9:00 a.m." can slip by. But clock times take "at": at 9:00 a.m.
